name: Omar al-Bayoumi

summary.text: Omar al-Bayoumi is a Saudi national who lived in San Diego and, in early 2000, helped the future hijackers Nawaf al-Hazmi and Khalid al-Mihdhar find an apartment after meeting them in Los Angeles. Official records describe him as carried on the books of the Saudi Civil Aviation Authority and paid by its contractor Dallah Avco with no apparent work. The 9/11 Commission (2004) found no credible evidence that he believed in violent extremism or knowingly aided extremist groups. A 2017 FBI memo released under Executive Order 14040 states that he received a monthly payment as a cooptee of Saudi General Intelligence; the FBI's Operation Encore closing material states that the evidence did not establish a knowing conspiracy. He has never been charged. He was arrested in Britain in September 2001 and released without charge, and the 9/11 families' lawsuit naming him was allowed to proceed in August 2025. Saudi Arabia denies that he was its asset.

facts.claim: A declassified CIA document, released in September 2020, describes al-Bayoumi as carried for decades on the employment books of the Saudi Civil Aviation Authority and paid by its contractor Dallah Avco, for which he did no apparent work; it says his salary payments were irregular and in varying amounts and were approved by a Civil Aviation Authority employee. In a 2003 interview he said he had come to the United States to study and to work for Dallah Avco.
facts.quote: He did no apparent work for this company, however.

sources.title: Possible Saudi government connections to the 9/11 plot or plotters

facts.claim: The 9/11 Commission's final report stated that it had seen no credible evidence that al-Bayoumi believed in violent extremism or knowingly aided extremist groups, and that neither at the time he helped the two hijackers find an apartment nor later did he give money to al-Hazmi or al-Mihdhar.
facts.quote: We have seen no credible evidence that he believed in violent extremism or knowingly aided extremist groups.

facts.claim: The declassified CIA document states that the documentary evidence that al-Bayoumi provided assistance to al-Hazmi and al-Mihdhar is solid, and records almost 100 telephone calls from al-Bayoumi to Saudi government offices in the United States between January 2000, when the two arrived in Los Angeles, and May 2000. The same document notes that the FBI had earlier found no evidence that he was an intelligence officer.
facts.quote: The documentary evidence that Bayoumi provided assistance to Hazmi and Mihdhar is solid

sources.title: Possible Saudi government connections to the 9/11 plot or plotters

facts.claim: A 2017 FBI memo, declassified under Executive Order 14040 and reported by CBS News, states that al-Bayoumi received a monthly payment as a cooptee of Saudi General Intelligence routed through then-Ambassador Prince Bandar bin Sultan, and that the earlier allegations about his intelligence ties were not confirmed at the time of the 9/11 Commission Report. A separate FBI memo assessed a 50/50 chance that he had advance knowledge of the attacks. These are FBI assessments, not findings of fact, and Saudi Arabia denies that he was its asset.
facts.quote: the earlier allegations about his Saudi intelligence ties were not confirmed at the time of the 9/11 Commission Report. The above information confirms these allegations.

sources.title: Documents responsive to Executive Order 14040, section 2(b)(ii)

facts.claim: The FBI's 2016 Operation Encore electronic communication, the first document released under Executive Order 14040, describes al-Bayoumi's assistance to the two hijackers as including translation, travel, lodging and financing, according to the memo as quoted in reporting; the casefile's closing material states that the evidence did not establish that he, al-Thumairy and al-Jarrah knowingly conspired to assist the hijackers, and he has never been charged.
facts.quote: Bayoumi's assistance to Hamzi and Midha included translation, travel, lodging and financing

Documents responsive to Executive Order 14040, section 2(b)(ii)

facts.claim: In 2024, evidence unsealed in the 9/11 families' lawsuit included a video seized from al-Bayoumi's Birmingham, England home in 2001 showing him filming the U.S. Capitol's architecture, entrances and security while referring to a plan; attorneys for Saudi Arabia described it as a tourist video and said a sketch of a plane in a notepad appeared to be a child's math assignment.
facts.quote: attorneys for the kingdom dismissed the Capitol "casing" film as a "tourist video that includes footage of artwork, flowerbeds, and a squirrel on the White House lawn."

connections.claim: A declassified CIA document describes al-Bayoumi as carried on the employment books of the Saudi Civil Aviation Authority and paid through its contractor Dallah Avco with no apparent work; in August 2025 Judge Daniels found the evidence supported a reasonable inference that his employment was more than his job title suggested. Saudi Arabia denies he was its agent.
connections.quote: carried for decades on the Saudi Civil Aviation Authority's employment books

connections.claim: The 9/11 Commission reported that al-Bayoumi met al-Thumairy at the Los Angeles consulate in February 2000, shortly before meeting the two hijackers at a restaurant, and that the two spoke by telephone numerous times about what al-Bayoumi said were religious matters.
connections.quote: al-Bayoumi said those calls concerned religious matters

openQuestions: The 2001 arrest in Britain and release without charge is widely reported but was not confirmed from a source reached in this session; it is in the summary only as context and should be checked.

The Dallah Avco employer and the 'Ercan' project name on the site were not confirmed beyond the CIA document; the 9/11 Commission's own wording on his job should be checked in the report's chapter 7 notes.
